title: Refined quasi-finite affine-space chart with purely transcendental image residue field
statement: Let $p:Z\to S$ be a finite type morphism of affine schemes [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], let $z\in Z$, put $s=p(z)$, and set $n=\dim_z(Z_s)$ [def-pc-fibre-product, def-weil-residue-field, def-kun-dimension]. There exist affine open neighbourhoods $S_0\subseteq S$ of $s$ and $Z_0\subseteq p^{-1}(S_0)$ of $z$, and an $S_0$-morphism $q:Z_0\to\mathbf A^n_{S_0}$ [def-sbc-affine-space], such that $q$ is quasi-finite (of finite type with finite discrete fibres) and, for $t=q(z)$, the induced extension $\kappa(t)/\kappa(s)$ is purely transcendental: it is isomorphic over $\kappa(s)$ to $\kappa(s)(u_1,\ldots,u_r)$ for some $0\le r\le n$. The dimension here is topological dimension at the point, not the dimension of its local ring.

source.place: Tag 0520, lemma-refined-quasi-finite-over-polynomial-algebra, and its scheme translation in more-morphisms.tex Tag 052E, first paragraph of proof. The prime in the polynomial algebra is (p,x_{r+1},...,x_n), hence has residue field kappa(p)(x_1,...,x_r).

proof.text: Write $S=\operatorname{Spec}R$, $Z=\operatorname{Spec}A$, and $R\to A$ for the finite-type ring map. Let $\mathfrak q_A$ represent $z$ and $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q_A\cap R$ represent $s$; put $k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra], $Z_s\cong\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_R k)$, with projection induced by $a\mapsto a\otimes1$. The prime over $z$ is the one specified by [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-ring-primes-residue-fields]. Under this scheme isomorphism, open neighbourhoods and chains of irreducible closed subsets correspond, so [def-kun-topological-dimension-at-point] identifies $n=\dim_z(Z_s)$ with the dimension at that fibre prime. Thus [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-finite-over-polynomial-algebra] gives $g\notin\mathfrak q_A$ and a finite-type map $\alpha:R[t_1,\ldots,t_n]\to B=A_g$ quasi-finite at every prime. Let $\mathfrak q_B=\mathfrak q_A B$, which contracts to $\mathfrak q_A$ by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-prime-residue-field-iso].

source.place: Tag 0520, first paragraph; Tag 00QE; Tags 01I4/01JQ, 00E6 and 0055 for the affine fibre and topological dimension

proof.text: Put $\mathfrak q'=\alpha^{-1}(\mathfrak q_B)$. Its contraction to $R$ is $\mathfrak p$. The polynomial scalar-extension isomorphism [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-scalar-extension] identifies $R[t]\otimes_Rk$ with $k[t]$. Let $Q\subset k[t]$ be the prime corresponding to $\mathfrak q'$. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-ring-primes-residue-fields], $\kappa(Q)\cong\kappa(\mathfrak q')$ over $k$; this is the residue field of the image in the original polynomial chart, rather than $\kappa(\mathfrak q_B)$. Set $r=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(Q)$. Apply [lem-trf-refined-noether-normalization-prime] to get a finite $k$-algebra map $\bar\psi:k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\to k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$ with $\bar\psi^{-1}(Q)=I=(x_{r+1},\ldots,x_n)$. Write $\bar h_i=\bar\psi(x_i)$.

source.place: Tag 0520, second paragraph; Tag 051P and the fibre-prime residue-field comparison

proof.text: Each of the finitely many coefficients in the polynomials $\bar h_i$ is the image of a fraction $a/b$ with $a\in R$ and $b\notin\mathfrak p$. Taking $f$ to be the product of these denominators (or $1$ if there are none) gives $f\notin\mathfrak p$ and lifts $h_i\in R_f[t]$. The polynomial universal property defines $\psi:C=R_f[x]\to D=R_f[t]$, $x_i\mapsto h_i$, whose scalar extension to $k$ is $\bar\psi$. The ring $D$ is finite type over $C$: the $t_j$ generate it as a $C$-algebra. Let $\mathfrak q_D=\mathfrak q'D$ and $P=\psi^{-1}(\mathfrak q_D)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-localization-prime-residue-field-iso], $\mathfrak q_D$ contracts to $\mathfrak q'$; therefore $P\cap R_f=\mathfrak pR_f$. The fibre-prime correspondence in [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-ring-primes-residue-fields] applied to $R_f\to C,D$ shows that the prime of $C\otimes_{R_f}k=k[x]$ corresponding to $P$ is $I$. Indeed, for $c\in C$, $\psi(c)\in\mathfrak q_D$ iff $\bar\psi(\bar c)\in Q$ iff $\bar c\in I$.

source.place: Tag 0520, lifting the normalized coordinates after inverting f

proof.text:
The residue-field comparison gives $\kappa(P)\cong\kappa(I)$ as $C$-algebras. Consequently the fibre of $\psi$ over $P$ is explicitly
$$D\otimes_C\kappa(P)\cong k[t]\otimes_{k[x]}\kappa(I).$$
The forward map sends $d\otimes a$ to $\bar d\otimes a$, using the residue-field comparison on $a$; its inverse sends $(d\otimes b)\otimes a$ to $d\otimes ba$, using the induced $k$-action on $\kappa(P)$. These maps respect the tensor relations and are inverse on pure tensors. They identify the primes belonging to $\mathfrak q_D$ and $Q$, since contracting either prime to $D$ gives $\mathfrak q_D$ and the fibre-prime correspondence is unique. A finite set of module generators for the finite map $\bar\psi$ tensors to generators of the right-hand side over $\kappa(I)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-finite-ring-map-quasi-finite], this finite algebra over the field has every spectrum point isolated: its only base fibre is itself. Thus the displayed fibre has its chosen prime isolated, which by [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime] says that $\psi$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q_D$. Now [lem-weil-pbc-ring-quasi-finite-locus-open] gives $h\in D\setminus\mathfrak q_D$ such that $C\to D_h$ is finite type and quasi-finite at every prime.

source.place: Tag 0520, finite special-fibre map implies quasi-finiteness at the prime; Tag 00QA supplies h

proof.text: First invert $f$ in both $R[t]$ and $B$, obtaining $D=R_f[t]\to B_f$. Next invert $h\in D$ in the source and its image $\alpha_f(h)$ in $B_f$, obtaining $D_h\to T=B_f[1/\alpha_f(h)]$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-finite-at-prime-principal-localization] twice: first with base element $f$ and target element $1$, then with base element $h$ and target element $1$. Every prime of $T$ contracts at each stage to a prime avoiding the inverted element, by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-prime-residue-field-iso], and the original map $\alpha$ is quasi-finite at each such prime. Therefore $D_h\to T$ is finite type and quasi-finite at every prime. Composition with $C\to D_h$ has the same properties by [lem-trf-quasi-finite-composition], the statement of Stacks 00PO. In particular $T$ inverts the image of $f$; it is the iterated localization customarily denoted $A_{gfh}$. More precisely write $\alpha_f(h)=a/(gf)^N$ in $A_{gf}$ with $a\in A$. Since $h\notin\mathfrak q_D$ and $\alpha_f^{-1}(\mathfrak q_B B_f)=\mathfrak q_D$, one has $a\notin\mathfrak q_A$. Then $T\cong A_{gfa}$, since $gf$ is already a unit and inverting $a/(gf)^N$ is equivalent to inverting $a$. Thus $Z_0=\operatorname{Spec}T$ and $S_0=\operatorname{Spec}R_f$ are principal affine opens containing $z,s$, and $Z_0\subseteq p^{-1}(S_0)$, by [lem-weil-pbc-principal-localization-open-immersion].

source.place: Tag 0520, last paragraph; Tag 077H for localization and Tag 00PO for composition

proof.text:
Let $\mathfrak q_T=\mathfrak q_A T$ represent $z$ in $Z_0$. Extension-contraction under localization [lem-weil-pbc-localization-prime-residue-field-iso] gives $\alpha_f^{-1}(\mathfrak q_B B_f)=\mathfrak q_D$ and contracts the prime of $T$ back to $\mathfrak q_B B_f$. Therefore the contraction of $\mathfrak q_T$ to $C$ is precisely $P=\psi^{-1}(\mathfrak q_D)$. Compute this ideal, rather than asserting it is unchanged. For every $F\in R_f[x]$, the fibre-prime correspondence gives
$$F\in P\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \bar\psi(\bar F)\in Q\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \bar F\in(x_{r+1},\ldots,x_n)\subset k[x].$$
The last condition says that all coefficients of $F(x_1,\ldots,x_r,0,\ldots,0)$ map to zero in $k$. The kernel of $R_f\to k$ is $\mathfrak pR_f$, so it is equivalent to $F\in(\mathfrak pR_f,x_{r+1},\ldots,x_n)$. Thus
$$P=(\mathfrak pR_f,x_{r+1},\ldots,x_n).$$
This proves the required prime contraction using the normalization statement, the lifted-coordinate square, and [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-ring-primes-residue-fields].

source.place: Tag 0520, prescribed inverse-image prime; Tags 00E6/0H9M and 00E3 for the fibre and localization prime correspondences

proof.text: The map $C\to T$ induces an $S_0$-morphism $q:Z_0\to\mathbf A^n_{S_0}$. It is locally quasi-finite by [pqf-def-quasifinite], since the same pair of affine charts works at every prime. The finite-type ring map gives a locally finite-type affine morphism. Its quasi-compactness can be checked on basic opens of $\operatorname{Spec}C$: the inverse image of $D(c)$ is $\operatorname{Spec}T_c$, which is quasi-compact by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-scheme-qcqs]; an affine open in the target is quasi-compact and therefore is a finite union of such basic opens. Thus [pqf-lem-qf-locqf-qc] makes $q$ quasi-finite. Equivalently its fibres are finite by [pqf-lem-qf-finitefibres]. The affine fibre formula [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] and the pointwise ring condition show that every singleton in each fibre is open, hence the finite fibres are discrete. This verifies the precise scheme formulation in the item.

source.place: Tag 052E, first paragraph: translate the affine chart to a quasi-finite scheme morphism; Tags 01TD, 02NH

proof.text: The image $t=q(z)$ is the point $P$ of $\operatorname{Spec}C$ computed in Step 6. Applied to $R_f\to C$ and its fibre prime $I$, [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-ring-primes-residue-fields] identifies $\kappa(t)=\kappa(P)$ with $\kappa(I)$ over $k$. Since $k[x]/I=k[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$, the residue field at $I$ is the fraction field $k(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$: localizing the quotient at its zero prime inverts exactly its nonzero elements. This equality follows directly from [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. The base residue field $\kappa(s)$ is $k$ even after replacing $R$ by $R_f$, by the residue-field clause of [lem-weil-pbc-localization-prime-residue-field-iso]. The number $r$ is nonnegative and at most $n$, since $\kappa(Q)$ is generated as a field by the images of the $n$ variables over $k$, so a transcendence basis has at most $n$ elements [def-kun-transcendence-degree]. Therefore $\kappa(t)/\kappa(s)$ is purely transcendental as required. No identification of the final $\kappa(t)$ with $\kappa(Q)$ or with the source $\kappa(z)$ occurs.
